title: Car Wash in Spain
subtitle: Market opportunity and unit economics of a forecourt car wash — ILLUSTRATIVE EXAMPLE
author: Aqmen
bottom_line: Spain's paid car-wash market is a ~€[1.1]bn serviceable market growing ~[4]% a year; a forecourt roll-wash of the flagship type pays back in ~[3.8] years at [55] cars/day, so the roll-out case holds if capture reaches ~[4]% of forecourt traffic.
exec_summary: [Client] has opened its flagship forecourt car wash and must decide how many sites to roll the format out to
Question: how big is the Spanish car-wash market, who competes for it, and does one more site pay back?
~[25]m cars, ~[60]% washed for pay at least once a year, ~[9] paid washes/yr at ~[8]€ → SAM ~€[1.1]bn; TAM (all washes at paid price) ~€[2.4]bn
Forecourts hold ~[45]% of paid washes; standalone chains ~[25]%; hand-wash and independents the rest
Growth ~[4]% p.a. to 2030, driven by premiumisation (ticket) and subscription models (frequency); water regulation caps the informal segment
Five archetypes: integrated fuel retailers, standalone automated chains, hand-wash networks, supermarket forecourts, independents
Fuel retailers win on convenience and traffic; standalone chains on quality and subscription; price is the least differentiating factor
Consolidation among standalone chains and the entry of subscription formats are the two trends that could pressure forecourt capture
Capex ~€[350]k per roll-wash; mature EBITDA ~€[140]k/yr at [55] cars/day and €[8.5] ticket → payback ~[3.8] yrs, IRR ~[22]%
Break-even at ~[28] cars/day; flagship is running at ~[48] cars/day after 8 weeks
Case is most sensitive to volume: ±10 cars/day moves payback by ~±0.9 years
need_to_believe: Capture rate of ~[4]% of forecourt vehicle traffic (flagship: [3.1]% after 8 weeks, rising)
Average ticket of ~€[8.5] holds with a ~[30]% premium-programme mix
Variable cost per wash of ~€[1.6] (water, chemicals, energy) at current tariffs
No standalone chain opens within [1.5] km of the site in the first three years
Fixed costs of ~€[95]k/yr including the opportunity cost of forecourt space

sections.title: Objective & scope
sections.headline: We size Spain's paid car-wash market and test whether one more forecourt wash pays back
body: In scope: paid washes of passenger cars and light vans in Spain — automated roll-over, tunnel, jet-wash bays and hand-wash
Out of scope: fleet/HGV washing, home washing (counted only in TAM), detailing
Geography: Spain, by autonomous community; horizon 2020–2030, annual; €
Company part: project economics of one forecourt roll-wash of the flagship type
so_whats: The decision is a roll-out count, so the market is sized where the sites are: forecourts
TAM includes home washing to show the whitespace paid formats can convert

sections.title: Data landscape
sections.headline: Public data covers the car parc and fuel-site network well; wash frequency and ticket rest on surveys
body: Strong: DGT car parc by province; fuel-station census (MITECO); supermarket forecourt counts
Moderate: operator counts and revenues for the main chains (filings, press)
Thin: paid-wash frequency and ticket — consumer surveys and the flagship's own data
so_whats: Where data is thin we estimate transparently and show the sensitivity
Flagship data is the best evidence on capture and ticket; eight weeks is short
sections.watchout: Frequency and ticket (confidence 2) drive ~70% of the SAM — see sensitivity
sections.source: DGT, MITECO, operator filings, consumer survey, aqmen

sections.title: Market expression & drivers
sections.headline: The market is cars × paid-wash penetration × frequency × ticket — four drivers, two of them uncertain
sections.chart_title: Spain car-wash market — expression & driver tree
sections.note: Each driver is estimated per region and per format (forecourt · standalone · hand-wash · supermarket); the cross-product is modelled, not shown.
so_whats: Car parc is known; penetration and frequency carry the judgement
Ticket is observable at the pump; mix between formats is not

sections.title: TAM and whitespace by region
sections.headline: TAM is ~€[2.4]bn if every wash were paid; the served market is ~€[1.1]bn, with the largest whitespace in the south and interior
sections.chart_title: Car-wash TAM by region, 2025 €m (SAM solid, whitespace hatched)
so_whats: Penetration is highest where forecourt density is highest
The south has the most unconverted washes per car — whitespace for paid formats

sections.title: Served market by format
sections.headline: Forecourts hold ~[45]% of the served market; standalone automated chains are the growing second format
so_whats: Forecourt leads every region; standalone is strongest where land is cheap and traffic dense
Hand-wash is a larger share in the south and islands — the informal segment to convert

sections.title: Trends
sections.headline: Six trends move the drivers; premiumisation and subscriptions lift the market, water rules squeeze the informal segment
sections.chart_title: Trends and the driver each one moves
rows: Ceramic/wax programmes lift average ticket ~[2]€ where offered
Subscribers wash [2–3]× more often; ~[8]% of users today
Bans on street and home washing push volume to recycling-equipped sites
EV owners visit forecourts less but wash more at destination sites
Fewer fuel visits reduce forecourt capture unless the wash is a destination
Scaled chains open near high-traffic forecourts with better equipment
so_whats: Net effect positive on value, mixed on forecourt share
The two forecourt-specific risks are fuel-visit decline and standalone entry

sections.title: Trajectory
sections.headline: The served market grows ~[4]% a year to ~€[1.35]bn by 2030, led by forecourt and standalone formats
so_whats: Standalone grows fastest (~[7]%); forecourt ~[4]%; hand-wash flat to declining
2020–22 dip and recovery tracks mobility

sections.title: Driver detail
sections.headline: Frequency does the work: paid washes per car rise from ~[8] to ~[10] a year as subscriptions spread
sections.chart_title: Paid washes per car per year and average ticket, €
so_whats: Penetration is near saturation in cities; growth is frequency and ticket
Both are the low-confidence drivers — hence the sensitivity

sections.title: Sensitivity
sections.headline: Frequency moves the SAM most: ±1 wash/yr is ±€[130]m
sections.chart_title: Sensitivity of 2025 SAM to key drivers, €m
so_whats: Prioritise evidence on frequency: loyalty-card data from the flagship
Mix matters less for size, more for who captures it

sections.title: Appendix — triangulation
sections.headline: Bottom-up and top-down agree within ~[8]% once fleet washing is removed from the trade figure
so_whats: Trade figure of €[1.5]bn includes fleets and detailing; ~€[300]m removed like-for-like
Supply-side build lands slightly low because independents are under-counted

sections.title: Appendix — sanity checks
sections.headline: The numbers hold up against simple ratios: ~€[45] per car per year and ~[60] washes per site per day
body: €[1.1]bn / [25]m cars = ~€[45] per car per year, or about one wash every six weeks at €[8]
~[9,000] wash sites nationally → ~[140]m washes / 9,000 / 300 days ≈ [52] washes per site per day
A tunnel at 60 washes/day for 12 hours is one car every 12 minutes — plausible for a forecourt, low for a dedicated chain
so_whats: Per-site throughput is consistent with the flagship's observed ~[48] cars/day
If anything the site count is high, which would lift throughput per site

sections.title: Scenario — subscription acceleration
sections.headline: If subscriptions reach ~[20]% of users by 2030, the SAM is ~€[1.5]bn rather than €[1.35]bn
body: Standalone chains and fuel retailers push unlimited plans; subscribers wash [2.5]× as often
Overrides vs Base (quantitative):
Washes / car / yr 2030: [11.5] (was [10.1])
Avg ticket 2030: €[8.6] (was €[9.0]) — plan pricing dilutes ticket
so_whats: Volume up, ticket down: the net is +[11]% on SAM
Forecourts only benefit if they run their own plan

sections.title: Player set & archetypes
sections.headline: Five archetypes compete for the wash: fuel retailers, standalone chains, hand-wash networks, supermarkets and independents
body: Integrated fuel retailers — [Client], [Competitor A], [Competitor B]: traffic-led, wash as an add-on to fuel and shop
Standalone automated chains — [Chain A], [Chain B]: quality- and subscription-led, destination sites
Hand-wash networks — [Network A]: labour-based, car-park and mall locations
Supermarket forecourts — [Retailer A], [Retailer B]: price-led, low service
Independents — ~[3,000] single-site operators, revenue-only in the build
so_whats: The economics differ by archetype, so benchmarks are within archetype
Fuel retailers and standalone chains contest the same premium customer

sections.title: Revenue build
sections.headline: The named players reconcile bottom-up to ~€[1.06]bn, close to the demand-side SAM
sections.chart_title: Player revenue build — revenue × % addressable = car-wash revenue, €m
so_whats: Fuel retailers hold ~[36]% between three players; standalone chains ~[21]%
Independents are a third of the market and the least visible — the conversion opportunity
sections.source: Operator filings, company websites, expert interviews, aqmen

sections.title: Archetype map
sections.headline: Archetypes separate on network reach and service depth; fuel retailers are broad and shallow, chains narrow and deep
so_whats: The whitespace is top-right: national reach with premium service — nobody holds it
A fuel retailer with a subscription programme moves right without losing reach

sections.title: Competitive trends
sections.headline: Standalone chains are consolidating and opening next to high-traffic forecourts; supermarkets compete on price only
body: [Chain A] acquired [n] regional operators in 2024–25; PE-backed, targeting [300] sites
New sites cluster within 1 km of top-decile forecourts — direct capture risk
Supermarkets hold price at €[5–6] and do not invest in equipment
Hand-wash networks are losing volume to water restrictions
so_whats: The threat is specific: a chain opening next to a good forecourt
Price competition from supermarkets does not reach the premium customer
sections.source: Press, operator announcements, expert interviews, aqmen

sections.title: Key buying factors
sections.headline: Convenience and quality decide the wash; price ranks last for the premium customer
so_whats: Fuel retailers win convenience by default; quality and loyalty are the gaps to close
Interviews rank convenience > quality > loyalty > speed > price

sections.title: Implications
sections.headline: A fuel retailer that matches chain quality and runs a subscription owns the whitespace; the risk is site-by-site entry
body: Whitespace: national reach + premium equipment + subscription — no archetype holds all three
Threat: standalone entry next to the best forecourts; mitigate with site selection and first-mover roll-out
So-what for the roll-out: prioritise sites with high traffic and no chain within 1.5 km
so_whats: The roll-out case is a race for the best sites
Subscription is the lever that turns traffic into frequency

sections.title: Reliability review
sections.headline: Coverage is strong on networks and pricing, thin on chain revenues and on independents
body: Strong: site counts, list prices, formats — observed
Moderate: chain revenues — filings for two, estimates for the rest
Weak: independents — count from the fuel-site census, revenue estimated
so_whats: Sparse cells are stated, not hidden
Independents' share is directional
sections.watchout: Independents' revenue (confidence 2) is ~30% of the build — treat their share as directional

sections.title: The investment case
sections.headline: One roll-wash of the flagship type costs ~€[350]k and reaches maturity in year 2
body: Capex €[350]k: equipment €[220]k, civil works and water recycling €[100]k, permits and signage €[30]k — CLIENT INPUT
Ramp-up: [60]% of mature volume in year 1, [90]% in year 2, mature from year 3
Asset life 10 years; maintenance capex [3]% of equipment per year
Site: existing forecourt; opportunity cost of space charged at €[20]k/yr
so_whats: Inputs from the client are separated from aqmen assumptions throughout
Opportunity cost of the forecourt space is included; the case is not flattered

sections.title: Unit economics
sections.headline: Site EBITDA is cars/day × ticket less ~€[1.6] variable per wash and ~€[95]k fixed — volume is the lever
sections.chart_title: One forecourt car wash — unit-economics tree (mature year)
sections.note: All values per site per year at maturity; volume tied to forecourt traffic × capture in the volume build.
so_whats: Cars/day is the only low-certainty leaf and the one the client can act on
Costs are observable; the argument is about volume

sections.title: Volume build
sections.headline: [55] cars/day is a ~[4]% capture of ~[1,400] daily forecourt vehicles — the flagship is at [3.1]% after eight weeks
body: Forecourt traffic ~[1,400] vehicles/day (fuel + shop) — CLIENT INPUT
Capture rate [4]% at maturity → [56] washes/day; flagship trend [2.2]% → [3.1]% over weeks 1–8
Cross-check vs market: [55]/day × 300 = [16.5]k washes ≈ [0.6]% of the regional SAM volume — plausible for one site
Subscription mix [15]% of washes adds ~[6] cars/day at maturity
so_whats: Capture is the assumption to track weekly; [4]% is within the range of comparable forecourt washes
Volume reconciles to the market: no implausible share

sections.title: P&L per site at maturity
sections.headline: At maturity a site converts ~€[280]k of revenue into ~€[140]k EBITDA and ~€[133]k cash after maintenance
so_whats: EBITDA margin ~[50]% at maturity; ~[35]% in year 1 during ramp-up
Fixed cost is two-thirds of the cost base — hence the volume sensitivity

sections.title: Cash flow & payback
sections.headline: Cumulative cash turns positive in year [4]: payback ~[3.8] years, IRR ~[22]%, NPV ~€[310]k at [9]%
sections.chart_title: Cash flow per site, €k (capex at t0)
so_whats: Discounted payback ~[4.6] years at a [9]% hurdle
Ramp-up costs about a year of payback; a faster ramp is worth more than a higher ticket

sections.title: Break-even
sections.headline: The site covers its fixed costs at ~[28] cars/day and reaches a [15]% IRR at ~[45] — the flagship already clears both
sections.chart_title: Cars per day required, vs flagship run-rate
so_whats: Break-even is half the base-case volume: the downside is a slow site, not a losing one
Flagship at week 8 already exceeds the 15% IRR threshold

sections.title: Sensitivity
sections.headline: Payback stays under [5] years for any ticket above €[7.5] if volume holds at [45]+ cars/day
so_whats: Volume dominates: 10 cars/day ≈ €0.5 of ticket
The case fails the hurdle only below ~[35] cars/day at a sub-€[7.5] ticket

sections.title: What you need to believe
sections.headline: Five assertions carry the case; two are already evidenced by the flagship, three need the next six months
body: Capture reaches ~[4]% of forecourt traffic — flagship [3.1]% and rising: PARTLY EVIDENCED
Ticket holds at ~€[8.5] with [30]% premium mix — flagship €[8.7]: EVIDENCED
Cost per wash ~€[1.6] at current water and energy tariffs — supplier quotes: EVIDENCED
No standalone chain opens within 1.5 km in years 1–3 — depends on site selection: TO MONITOR
Fixed cost ~€[95]k incl. space — needs the space charge agreed internally: TO CONFIRM
so_whats: The roll-out decision hinges on capture; track it weekly on the flagship
Site selection is the main control over the competitive risk

sections.title: Scenario — chain opens nearby
sections.headline: A standalone chain within 1 km cuts capture to ~[3]% and stretches payback to ~[5.5] years
body: A quality-led chain opens next to the forecourt and takes the premium customer
Overrides vs Base (quantitative):
Cars/day at maturity: [42] (was [55])
Average ticket: €[8.0] (was €[8.5]) — premium mix falls
so_whats: Still above EBITDA break-even; IRR falls to ~[13]%
Argues for a subscription offer at launch, not later
